tagline: A sequence of love poems between a woman and a man, celebrating desire, delight, and faithful love, which Jews and Christians have also long read as a song of God's love for his people.
overview:
The Song of Songs is a book of poetry about love between a woman and a man. There is no law in it, no prophecy, no history of kings and battles, and God's name does not clearly appear in it. Instead two lovers speak to each other and about each other: they long for each other when apart, search for each other through the city at night, praise each other's bodies in lavish images drawn from gardens, vineyards, mountains, spices, and jewels, and at last declare that love is as strong as death. A group the woman calls the daughters of Jerusalem listens in and sometimes answers. The woman speaks more of the lines than anyone else, and her voice, eager, frank, and unashamed, sets the tone of the whole book.

The title means the finest or greatest song, in the way that holy of holies means the most holy place. For most of its history the book was read by Jews and Christians alike as an allegory: in the synagogue, a song of the love between God and Israel; in the church, a song of Christ and the church or Christ and the individual soul. Since the nineteenth century most interpreters have read it first as what it plainly appears to be, poetry celebrating human love and sexual desire within a committed bond. Many readers today hold both together, reading the Song as a celebration of married love that also, by its place in Scripture, points beyond itself to the love of God.

The Song matters because it refuses to treat the body and desire as shameful or merely useful. It sits in the Bible as a witness that the love of a man and a woman is God's good gift, worth singing about, and also as a warning that love is a fire too strong to be stirred up carelessly. Readers who have been taught only silence or suspicion about sexuality often find it startling. Readers who have been taught that desire is the whole of life find it just as startling, because it binds desire to faithfulness.
author:
The first verse reads “This is Solomon’s Song of Songs.” The Hebrew phrase can mean a song by Solomon, but it can also mean a song for, about, or dedicated to Solomon, and the same construction in the Psalms (for David) is debated in the same way. Jewish and Christian tradition generally took Solomon as the author. First Kings 4:32 says that Solomon composed 1,005 songs and speaks of his knowledge of plants and animals, which fits the Song's rich world of trees, flowers, and creatures. Solomon is named several times in the book (1:5; 3:7, 9, 11; 8:11-12), and a king appears in 1:4, 1:12, and 7:5.

Many scholars, including some conservative ones, think Solomon is a figure within the poems rather than their author. They note that he is sometimes spoken of from the outside, and in 8:11-12 his wealth seems to be set aside in favor of the woman's own freely given love. On this view an unnamed poet, or a collector of love poems, used the famous king as a symbol of splendor and romance. Others read the royal references as a genuine sign of Solomonic origin or of composition in his court. The book does not settle the question, and its meaning does not depend on it.
date: Those who hold to Solomonic authorship place the Song in the tenth century BC. Many modern scholars date its final form later, in the Persian period (fifth or fourth century BC) or the early Greek period, pointing to its Hebrew: it uses a short form of the relative word that is more common in later Hebrew, some forms resembling Aramaic, and what looks like a Persian loanword, pardes, orchard (4:13), the word behind the English paradise. Others answer that these features may reflect the dialect of northern Israel or the conventions of love poetry rather than a late date, and they note that the mention of Tirzah alongside Jerusalem (6:4) makes most sense before about 880 BC, when Tirzah was still a royal city of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:23-24). Some think the book gathers older poems that were edited over time. The range of proposals runs from the tenth to the third century BC.
setting:
The Song moves between two worlds. One is the countryside of Israel: vineyards and orchards, flocks of goats and sheep, gazelles and deer on the hills, spring rains and blossoming vines, and places from the far north (Lebanon, Hermon, Gilead) to the oasis of En-gedi by the Dead Sea. The other is the city and the royal court of Jerusalem, with its streets and watchmen, its walls and towers, its perfumes, gold, ivory, and purple cloth. The lovers move freely between these worlds, and the poems use both to praise each other.

Ancient Israel's neighbors also wrote love poetry. The closest parallels are Egyptian love songs from the New Kingdom period (roughly 1300 to 1100 BC), preserved on papyri and pottery, in which the lovers call each other brother and sister, praise each other's bodies, and complain of lovesickness, all as the Song does. Mesopotamian texts also contain love poetry, some of it tied to the worship of gods and goddesses. An older theory that the Song began as a pagan fertility liturgy has found little support. What sets the Song apart is its setting within Israel's faith, where love and marriage belong to the good order of creation rather than to the service of fertility gods.
purpose: Read as love poetry, the Song celebrates the goodness of desire and delight between a man and a woman, teaches the power of love and the need to guard it until its time, and honors a love that is mutual, exclusive, and lasting. It gives God's people words for a part of life that Scripture elsewhere often mentions only in warnings. Read as the synagogue and the church read it for centuries, it also gives words for the longing of God's people for God and his delight in them. Jewish communities read the Song at Passover, the feast that remembers God's rescue of Israel from Egypt, as one of the five short books (the Megillot) read at the festivals. The Song gives no statement of purpose, so these purposes are inferred from what it says and from how it has been used.
story: The Song belongs to the Bible's wisdom and poetry books, alongside Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes, and in the Hebrew Bible it stands among the Writings. It follows naturally after Genesis 2, where God brings the woman to the man and they are naked and unashamed, and after Genesis 3, where that ease is broken. The Song pictures love in a garden again, with a freedom and joy that echo Eden. The prophets used marriage as a picture of God's covenant with Israel (Hosea 1 to 3, Isaiah 54 and 62, Ezekiel 16), and the New Testament carries that picture forward: Paul calls marriage a mystery that speaks of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31-32), and the Bible ends with the wedding supper of the Lamb and a bride prepared for her husband (Revelation 19 and 21).
christ: The New Testament never quotes the Song of Songs directly, so any link to Christ is drawn from the wider biblical theme of God as bridegroom rather than from a prediction in the book. That theme is strong: Jesus calls himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19-20), John the Baptist calls himself the bridegroom's friend (John 3:29), Paul reads marriage as a picture of Christ's self-giving love for the church (Ephesians 5:25-32), and Revelation closes with the marriage of the Lamb. The long Christian tradition, from Origen in the third century to Bernard of Clairvaux in the twelfth and many Puritan preachers later, read the Song as a portrait of Christ's love for the church and the believer's love for him. Readers who take the Song first as human love poetry often make a related point in a different way: a love that is exclusive, self-giving, and as strong as death (8:6) is itself a reflection of the love God shows in Christ, and every faithful marriage is meant to be a small picture of it.
reading:
Read the Song as poetry, not as a story with a clear plot or a manual with rules. Its images are meant to evoke feeling and beauty, not to be pictured literally: when he says her hair is like a flock of goats streaming down Mount Gilead, he means the dark, rippling movement of her hair, not the look of goats. Watch who is speaking, which the Hebrew often marks by whether a word is masculine or feminine; many translations add headings for the woman, the man, and the friends, but those headings are editorial guesses. Watch for the refrains: the charge not to awaken love until the time is right (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), the declarations of mutual belonging (2:16; 6:3; 7:10), and the scenes of seeking and finding.

Interpreters differ over how the poems fit together. Some read a loose story of courtship, wedding, and married life, with the wedding at the center (3:6-5:1). Some read two main characters, the woman and the man, who is pictured sometimes as a king and sometimes as a shepherd; others, following a view proposed in the nineteenth century, read three, with the woman remaining faithful to her shepherd lover while Solomon tries to win her. Still others read an anthology of separate love poems joined by shared imagery. The allegorical reading, the natural reading, and the combined reading are each held by faithful Jews and Christians. The frank language is part of the book's point; it speaks with adult tact, through images rather than explicit description, and a reader should neither be embarrassed by it nor make it cruder than it is.

structure.title: Title
structure.summary: The superscription names the book the Song of Songs, the finest of songs, and connects it with Solomon.

structure.title: Longing and first delight
structure.summary: The woman longs for her beloved, explains her sun-darkened skin, and the lovers trade praise until she rests in his embrace and gives the first charge not to awaken love too soon.

structure.title: The spring invitation and the night search
structure.summary: He comes leaping over the hills to call her away into the springtime; later she searches the city at night, finds him, and repeats the charge.

structure.title: The royal wedding
structure.summary: Solomon's wedding procession arrives, the man praises his bride from head to breast, calls her a locked garden, and at her invitation enters his garden.

structure.title: Absence and praise
structure.summary: She hesitates to open to him, he departs, and she searches and is beaten by the watchmen; asked what makes him special, she praises him from head to foot, and they are reunited.

structure.title: Admiration and invitation
structure.summary: He praises her again as unique among all women, and she invites him to the countryside and longs to love him openly.

structure.title: Love as strong as death
structure.summary: The climax declares love stronger than death and beyond price, followed by closing scenes about a little sister, Solomon's vineyard, and a final call to the beloved.

themes.title: Love and desire as God's good gift
themes.body: The Song celebrates physical beauty, attraction, and the delight of lovers in each other without embarrassment. Its gardens and vineyards echo Eden, where God made the man and the woman for each other and called his creation very good. The book assumes that sexual love, rightly ordered, belongs to that goodness and deserves to be sung.

themes.title: Mutuality
themes.body: The woman is no silent object. She speaks first and most, initiates, invites, and praises him as fully as he praises her. The refrains of belonging run both ways: “My beloved is mine and I am his” (2:16). In a world where marriage was often arranged around property and power, the Song pictures a love of two persons who choose each other.

themes.title: The right time
themes.body: Three times the woman charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to arouse or awaken love until the time is right. Love is powerful, and the Song treats it as something to be guarded as well as enjoyed. Much of the Christian and Jewish tradition has read this as a call to patience and chastity, keeping the full expression of love for its proper setting.

themes.title: Exclusive and faithful love
themes.body: The woman is a garden locked up and a fountain sealed (4:12), open to one lover alone, and she asks him to set her as a seal over his heart (8:6). Among sixty queens and eighty concubines, his dove is unique (6:8-9). The Song's love is not casual; it is jealous in the good sense, claiming and giving the whole person.

themes.title: Love stronger than death
themes.body: The climax (8:6-7) calls love as strong as death, a fire that many waters cannot quench and that no fortune can buy. Some readers hear in the Hebrew word for its flame a final syllable that may be a short form of God's name, though many take it as a way of saying the fiercest flame. Either way, the Song ends by claiming for love a strength and worth that point beyond the lovers themselves.

keyChapters.why: The opening longing, the woman's own voice, and the first images of vineyard, flock, and king set the world of the whole book.
The spring invitation, the refrain of mutual belonging, and the first charge not to awaken love until the time is right.
The groom's praise of his bride and the image of the locked garden, the heart of the wedding sequence.
The night of hesitation and loss, and the woman's great poem of praise for her beloved.
The climax: love as strong as death, which many waters cannot quench and no wealth can buy.
